Bias:
# Bias
## Bias as a concept
Bias is a systematic error or tendency that distorts thinking, behaviour or research. In the IB course it is one of six concepts used to analyse psychology. Cognitive biases are errors in thinking, such as confirmation bias, the tendency to look for information that supports existing beliefs.

## Bias in research
Researcher bias is when the researcher's expectations influence results. Participant bias includes demand characteristics, when participants guess the aim and change their behaviour, and social desirability bias, when they answer to look good. Sampling bias makes a sample unrepresentative. Bias is reduced with double-blind procedures, random sampling, standardized procedures and triangulation.

## Key terms
Bias: a systematic error that distorts thinking or research
Confirmation bias: looking for information that supports existing beliefs
Demand characteristics: participants changing behaviour after guessing the aim
Social desirability bias: answering to look good
Double-blind procedure: neither participants nor researchers know the condition
Causality:
# Causality
## Causality
Causality is the relationship between a cause and its effect. Only true experiments, in which the researcher manipulates an independent variable and controls other variables, can establish cause and effect. Correlational studies show relationships but not causation, because of third variables or reverse causation.

## Explaining behaviour
Behaviour usually has many interacting causes: biological, cognitive and sociocultural. Reductionism explains behaviour by one simple cause; holism looks at the whole system. Bidirectional ambiguity means it is unclear which variable causes which.

## Key terms
Causality: the relationship between a cause and its effect
Independent variable: the variable the researcher manipulates
Dependent variable: the variable that is measured
Correlation: a relationship between two variables, not proof of cause
Reductionism: explaining behaviour by one simple cause
Third variable: an unmeasured variable that affects both measured variables
Change:
# Change
## Change
Change is how individuals, groups and behaviour develop or are altered over time. Psychology studies change through development, learning, therapy and cultural change. Neuroplasticity is the brain's ability to change its structure and function in response to experience.

## Studying change
Longitudinal studies follow the same participants over time; cross-sectional studies compare different groups at one time. Interventions and treatments aim to bring about change, such as therapy for depression. Acculturation is the change that happens when cultures meet.

## Key terms
Neuroplasticity: the brain’s ability to change with experience
Longitudinal study: a study following the same participants over time
Cross-sectional study: a study comparing different groups at one time
Acculturation: cultural change when cultures meet
Intervention: an action designed to change behaviour or health
Measurement:
# Measurement
## Measurement
Measurement is how psychologists turn behaviour and mental processes into data. Quantitative data are numerical; qualitative data are descriptive. An operationalized variable is defined so it can be measured. Measures include questionnaires, observations, interviews, brain scans and reaction times.

## Quality of measurement
Reliability is the consistency of a measure; validity is whether it measures what it claims to. Internal validity is whether the study measured the effect of the independent variable; external validity is whether results generalize. Ecological validity is how well results apply to real life.

## Key terms
Operationalization: defining a variable so it can be measured
Reliability: the consistency of a measure
Validity: whether a measure measures what it claims
Ecological validity: how well results apply to real life
Quantitative data: numerical data
Qualitative data: descriptive data in words
Perspective:
# Perspective
## Perspective
Perspective is the point of view from which behaviour is explained. Different approaches — biological, cognitive and sociocultural — give different perspectives on the same behaviour. Emic approaches study a culture from the inside; etic approaches study it from the outside with universal measures.

## Using perspectives
Good explanations combine perspectives, such as the biopsychosocial model of health. Cultural perspective matters because most research comes from WEIRD samples: Western, educated, industrialized, rich and democratic.

## Key terms
Perspective: the point of view from which behaviour is explained
Emic approach: studying a culture from the inside
Etic approach: studying a culture from the outside
Biopsychosocial model: explaining health through biological, psychological and social factors
WEIRD: Western, educated, industrialized, rich and democratic samples
Responsibility:
# Responsibility
## Responsibility
Responsibility is the duty of psychologists to act ethically towards participants, clients and society. Ethical guidelines include informed consent, protection from harm, the right to withdraw, confidentiality, avoiding deception where possible and debriefing.

## Wider responsibility
Psychologists are responsible for how research is applied and reported, such as avoiding harm to vulnerable groups and stigma. Animal research must reduce, refine and replace (the 3Rs). Socially sensitive research has consequences for the groups studied.

## Key terms
Informed consent: agreeing to take part with full knowledge of the study
Debriefing: telling participants the true aims after a study
Right to withdraw: participants can leave the study at any time
Confidentiality: keeping participants’ data private
Deception: misleading participants about the study
The biological approach:
# The biological approach
## Assumptions
The biological approach explains behaviour through the brain, hormones, genes and evolution. Localization of function is the idea that specific brain areas have specific functions, such as Broca's area for speech production. Neurotransmitters are chemical messengers between neurons, such as serotonin and dopamine. Hormones are chemicals released by glands into the blood, such as cortisol and oxytocin.

## Genes and research
Twin studies compare monozygotic and dizygotic twins to estimate the role of genes. Heritability is the proportion of variation in a trait due to genetic differences. Brain imaging techniques include fMRI, which measures blood flow, and EEG. Animal research is used where human studies would be unethical.

## Key terms
Localization of function: specific brain areas having specific functions
Neurotransmitter: a chemical messenger between neurons
Hormone: a chemical released into the blood by a gland
Twin study: comparing identical and non-identical twins
Heritability: the share of variation due to genetic differences
fMRI: brain imaging that measures blood flow
The cognitive approach:
# The cognitive approach
## Assumptions
The cognitive approach explains behaviour through mental processes such as memory, perception, thinking and decision-making. The multi-store model of memory has a sensory store, short-term memory and long-term memory. The working memory model divides short-term memory into the central executive, phonological loop and visuospatial sketchpad.

## Thinking and reliability
Schema theory states that mental frameworks from experience shape how we process information. Reconstructive memory means memories are rebuilt each time, so they can be distorted, as shown by Loftus and Palmer's study of leading questions. Dual-process models describe fast, intuitive thinking (system 1) and slow, rational thinking (system 2).

## Key terms
Schema: a mental framework from experience
Multi-store model: a model of sensory, short-term and long-term memory
Working memory model: a model of short-term memory with several components
Reconstructive memory: memories rebuilt each time they are recalled
System 1 thinking: fast, intuitive thinking
The sociocultural approach:
# The sociocultural approach
## Assumptions
The sociocultural approach explains behaviour through the influence of other people, groups and culture. Social identity theory states that people gain self-esteem from group membership, leading to in-group favouritism. Social learning theory states that behaviour is learned by observing and imitating models, as in Bandura's Bobo doll study.

## Culture
Culture is the shared beliefs, norms and practices of a group. Cultural dimensions, such as individualism versus collectivism (Hofstede), describe differences between cultures. Enculturation is learning one's own culture; acculturation is adapting to a new one. Conformity is changing behaviour to match a group, as in Asch's study.

## Key terms
Social identity theory: self-esteem gained from group membership
Social learning theory: learning by observing and imitating models
Culture: shared beliefs, norms and practices of a group
Individualism: a cultural focus on personal goals
Collectivism: a cultural focus on group goals
Conformity: changing behaviour to match a group
Research methods and data:
# Research methods and data
## Methods
Experimental methods include laboratory, field and natural experiments. Quantitative non-experimental methods include correlational studies and surveys. Qualitative methods include interviews, observations, focus groups and case studies. Sampling methods include random, opportunity, self-selected and snowball sampling.

## Analysing data
Descriptive statistics summarize data: mean, median, mode, range and standard deviation. Inferential statistics test whether results are significant, usually at p < 0.05. Triangulation uses several methods or researchers to check findings. Credibility, transferability and reflexivity are used to judge qualitative research.

## Key terms
Laboratory experiment: an experiment in a controlled setting
Natural experiment: an experiment where the independent variable occurs naturally
Opportunity sampling: using people who are available
Inferential statistics: tests of whether results are significant
Triangulation: checking findings with several methods
Reflexivity: the researcher reflecting on their own influence
Health and well-being:
# Health and well-being
## The context
Health and well-being studies factors that influence physical and mental health. Well-being is a state of feeling good and functioning well. Explanations of health problems such as stress, depression and addiction combine biological, cognitive and sociocultural factors.

## Examples
Stress is the response to demands that exceed one's ability to cope, involving the HPA axis and cortisol. Depression is a mood disorder with persistent low mood; explanations include serotonin levels, negative cognitive schemas (Beck) and social factors. Treatments include medication such as SSRIs, cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) and health promotion. Prevalence is the proportion of a population with a condition.

## Key terms
Well-being: feeling good and functioning well
Stress: a response to demands that exceed coping ability
Cognitive behavioural therapy: therapy that changes unhelpful thoughts and behaviour
SSRI: an antidepressant that increases serotonin availability
Prevalence: the proportion of a population with a condition
Human development:
# Human development
## The context
Human development studies how people change across the lifespan, physically, cognitively and socially. Developmental psychology looks at nature and nurture, critical periods and the influence of family and culture.

## Examples
Attachment is the emotional bond between an infant and caregiver; Bowlby argued it is innate, and Ainsworth's Strange Situation identified secure and insecure types. Piaget proposed stages of cognitive development. Theory of mind is the ability to understand that others have different beliefs. Poverty and trauma can affect brain development.

## Key terms
Attachment: the emotional bond between an infant and caregiver
Strange Situation: Ainsworth’s procedure for classifying attachment
Theory of mind: understanding that others have different beliefs
Critical period: a time when certain development must happen
Nature–nurture debate: genes versus environment in development
Human relationships:
# Human relationships
## The context
Human relationships studies how relationships form, are maintained and break down, and how people interact in groups. It includes personal relationships, group dynamics and social responsibility.

## Examples
Explanations of attraction include similarity, proximity and evolutionary factors. Communication patterns, such as those studied by Gottman, predict relationship success. Group dynamics include cooperation, competition, prejudice and discrimination; Sherif's Robbers Cave study showed that competition increases conflict and superordinate goals reduce it. Prosocial behaviour is behaviour that helps others; the bystander effect is when people are less likely to help when others are present.

## Key terms
Prosocial behaviour: behaviour that helps others
Bystander effect: people being less likely to help when others are present
Prejudice: a negative attitude towards a group
Superordinate goal: a shared goal that requires cooperation
Attraction: what draws people to each other
Learning and cognition:
# Learning and cognition
## The context
Learning and cognition studies how people learn, remember, think and make decisions, and how this can be improved. It draws on cognitive, biological and sociocultural explanations.

## Examples
Classical conditioning is learning by association (Pavlov); operant conditioning is learning by reinforcement and punishment (Skinner). Memory can be improved by retrieval practice and spacing. Emotion affects cognition, as in flashbulb memories. Digital technology affects attention and memory. Heuristics are mental shortcuts that speed up decisions but can cause errors.

## Key terms
Classical conditioning: learning by association
Operant conditioning: learning by reinforcement and punishment
Heuristic: a mental shortcut
Flashbulb memory: a vivid memory of an emotional event
Retrieval practice: recalling information to strengthen memory
Paper 1:
# Paper 1
## The paper
Paper 1 assesses the approaches and concepts through the contexts. It includes short-answer questions and an extended response in which you explain and evaluate a behaviour using one or more approaches and concepts.

## How to answer
Command terms matter: describe means give a detailed account; explain means give reasons; evaluate means weigh strengths and limitations; discuss means offer a balanced review. Use named studies with aim, method, results and conclusion, and link them to the question. Evaluate studies on methods, ethics, generalizability and culture.

## Key terms
Command term: a word that tells you what kind of answer is needed
Evaluate: weigh strengths and limitations
Discuss: offer a balanced review
Generalizability: how far results apply beyond the sample
Paper 2:
# Paper 2
## The paper
Paper 2 assesses research methods and data. You analyse unseen research, interpret data and evaluate research designs, and in some questions design or improve a study.

## How to answer
Identify the method, design, sampling and variables. Comment on reliability, validity, ethics and bias. Interpret graphs and statistics, such as means, standard deviations and correlation coefficients. Suggest realistic improvements and explain why they would help.

## Key terms
Research design: the plan for how a study is carried out
Independent samples design: different participants in each condition
Repeated measures design: the same participants in every condition
Standard deviation: a measure of spread around the mean
Paper 3: HL:
# Paper 3: HL
## The paper
Paper 3 is the HL paper. It uses a class inquiry and unseen material to assess HL extensions: the role of culture, the role of motivation and the role of technology in human behaviour.

## How to prepare
Study how culture, motivation and technology affect behaviour in each context. Use evidence from research and evaluate it. Answers should apply concepts such as bias, causality and perspective to unseen scenarios.

## Key terms
HL extension: the HL topics of culture, motivation and technology
Motivation: what drives behaviour
Class inquiry: an investigation the class carries out together
Unseen material: new research or scenarios given in the exam
Internal assessment: research proposal a:
# Internal assessment: research proposal and report
## The internal assessment
The internal assessment asks you to propose and carry out a research study, and write a report. You choose a research question, justify your method, collect and analyse data, and evaluate your findings.

## Doing it well
State a clear, focused research question and operationalize the variables. Justify the design, sample and materials, and follow ethical guidelines. Present descriptive and inferential statistics or qualitative analysis. Evaluate strengths and limitations and suggest improvements. A hypothesis is a testable prediction.

## Key terms
Research question: the focused question your study answers
Hypothesis: a testable prediction
Null hypothesis: the prediction that there is no effect
Materials: the items used to carry out the study
